question: With a limit of 100 req/min using the Fixed Window algorithm — what is the maximum actual load a client can generate in 2 seconds at the boundary of two windows?

options.explanation: Fixed Window counts requests within each window separately. At the boundary of two windows (last second + first second), the client can use the limit of both windows

options.text: 200 requests — 100 at the end of the old window + 100 at the start of the new
options.explanation: This is boundary burst — the main drawback of Fixed Window. A client sends 100 requests at 00:59 (still within window 1) and 100 requests at 01:00 (already a new window 2). Total: 200 requests in ~2 seconds with a 100/min limit. Sliding Window Counter solves this with weighted counting
Fixed Window doesn't average. Each window has its own independent counter. The client gets the full limit in each window, so 2x is possible at the boundary

options.text: 50 requests — the limit is split between windows
options.explanation: Windows don't share the limit. Each window is an independent counter with the full limit. That's why a burst of up to 200 requests is possible at the boundary

question: Two API servers simultaneously execute GET counter → 99 (< 100) → INCR counter. What will happen and how to fix it?

options.text: Both requests will get 429 — Redis detects the conflict
options.explanation: Redis doesn't track conflicts on separate GET and INCR commands. Each command executes independently. Both GETs return 99, both INCRs execute successfully, counter becomes 101

options.text: No problem — Redis is single-threaded and processes commands sequentially
options.explanation: Redis is indeed single-threaded, but GET and INCR are separate commands. Between the GET from server A and its INCR, Redis can process the GET from server B. Atomicity is needed at the level of the entire operation (check + increment), not individual commands

options.text: Both requests will pass, counter becomes 101 — limit violated. Fix: use a Redis Lua script for atomic check-and-increment
options.explanation: This is a classic race condition in distributed systems. GET + check + INCR are three separate operations. Between GET and INCR, another server can execute its own GET and also see 99. A Lua script in Redis executes atomically — no other command can execute between the script's lines

options.text: Redis automatically blocks the second request through optimistic locking
options.explanation: Redis doesn't apply automatic locking on GET + INCR. WATCH/MULTI/EXEC provides optimistic locking, but a Lua script is simpler and more reliable: it executes atomically without the need for retries

question: Why is the Redis rate limiter implemented via a Lua script rather than a MULTI/EXEC transaction?

options.text: Lua scripts are 10x faster than MULTI/EXEC
options.explanation: The speed difference is minimal — both mechanisms execute within a single Redis event loop. The key difference is that Lua scripts support conditional logic (if/then), while MULTI/EXEC does not

options.text: MULTI/EXEC doesn't allow using the result of one command to make a decision in another — it's not a true transaction with conditional logic
options.explanation: MULTI/EXEC in Redis is a batch, not a transaction in the classical sense. All commands inside MULTI are queued and executed at once, but you cannot read the result of a GET and use it in an IF within the transaction. A Lua script allows: read value → compare with limit → decide whether to INCR or not — all atomically

options.text: Lua scripts are automatically replicated, while MULTI/EXEC is not
options.explanation: Both mechanisms are replicated in Redis. The advantage of Lua is conditional logic: you can read a value and based on it decide whether to increment or not
MULTI/EXEC supports EXPIRE. The problem is different: within MULTI, you cannot read the current counter value and make a decision based on it. All commands are queued blindly

question: In a production API with IP-based, user-based, and endpoint-based rate limits — in what order should they be checked and why?

options.text: User-based first — it's the most important limit for business
options.explanation: User-based is important, but checking requires authorization (extracting userId from a token). If a DDoS comes from thousands of IPs without a valid token, user-based limits won't help. Global and IP limits block such attacks more cheaply and earlier

options.text: From narrowest to broadest: endpoint → user → IP → global. Narrower limits are more accurate
options.explanation: This is inefficient: endpoint limit requires path parsing and authorization. If the system is under DDoS (global limit), checking the endpoint for every request is a waste of resources. Broader limits are cheaper and block coarse attacks earlier

options.text: Order doesn't matter — all checks are executed in parallel
options.explanation: Parallel checking creates unnecessary load on Redis: 4 calls instead of 1 (if the first limit is already exhausted). Additionally, you must wait for all responses before deciding. Sequential checking 'from cheap to expensive' is more optimal

options.text: From broadest to narrowest: global → IP → user → endpoint. Broader limits are cheaper to check and block coarse attacks before expensive checks
options.explanation: The 'funnel' principle: the global limit (one key in Redis) is the cheapest — it blocks DDoS before checking individual users. IP limit (no authorization needed) is cheaper than user limit (needs auth). Endpoint limit — the most detailed and expensive. If the global limit is already exhausted, there's no point checking the rest
